text: From a high camp in the basin below Mesahchie Peak, climbers side-hill traverse west along Kimtah's south face at roughly 7,400-7,600 ft, crossing more than a dozen loose ribs and gullies (mostly class 3). A well-known 'red ledge' cuts across the ribs and greatly simplifies the route-finding. Near the 'Grotesque Gendarmes,' the standard line downclimbs about 150 ft down a buttress and threads a narrow, exposed class 4 gully to bypass a cliff band, then regains the traverse. A final broad, solid-granite gully (class 3) leads up to the ridge just west of the true summit, finishing with a short class 3 scramble across a scree saddle between the west and east (true, 8,649 ft) summits.

edits.new: A final broad gully of solid granite (class 3) climbs to the ridge immediately west of the true summit

text: Regain the ~7,400 ft traverse level, then climb an obvious solid-granite gully to the ridge just west of the summit, finishing with class 3 scrambling across a scree saddle to the true (east) summit at 8,649 ft.

text: From the basin camp south of Mesahchie Peak, gain roughly 800 ft to a bench near 7,400 ft, then traverse west holding somewhere between 7,400 and 7,600 ft. The traverse is an endless maze of ribs and gullies and you will cross easily over a dozen of them. The hardest section is a rib about halfway along: drop to around 7,200 ft and look for two ledges that give passage, at the cost of some elevation to regain and a short stretch of class 4. Where a line looks like the easiest way through, it usually goes. There is no reliable water past the basin camp late in the season.

edits.old: The traverse is an endless maze of ribs and gullies and you will cross easily over a dozen of them.
edits.new: Expect a never-ending tangle of ribs and gullies along the traverse; you will cross well over a dozen.

text: The red ledge is the proof, and it is obvious when you are on it. Somewhere along the westward traverse the ground organises itself into one reddish ledge that cuts straight across every rib and gully — it runs almost like a trail, and it is the feature that makes this traverse reasonable instead of desperate. It crosses at the base of a couple of the Grotesque Gendarmes, the ragged towers standing on the crest above you, then carries on across roughly 7,800 ft through a cliffy cave section and delivers you to a couple of gullies that lead to the summit. If you are picking your way up and down individual ribs and gullies with no continuous ledge underfoot, you are above or below the line and should hunt for it rather than force the terrain. Take the broad, solid-granite gully to the ridge just west of the true summit; from its top a short class 3 scramble crosses a scree saddle east to the true top.

edits.old: It crosses at the base of a couple of the Grotesque Gendarmes
edits.new: It runs along the foot of a couple of the Grotesque Gendarmes

text: The maintained trail ends at White Pass. Traverse north below the White Mountain ridge into Foam Basin and White River Meadows, the usual base camp, either by way of Red Pass or by crossing snowfields to the notch west of Point 6770 and dropping into the White Chuck basin. From camp climb to Foam Pass and cross the White Chuck Glacier to the gap — this is glacier travel on largely featureless snow, so carry a track or the navigation skill to retrace it in cloud, and be roped for the crevasses low on the glacier, which can be fully open.

edits.new: either via Red Pass or by crossing snowfields toward the notch lying west of Point 6770 and descending into the White Chuck basin

text: The standard approach follows the North Fork Sauk River Trail (USFS Trail #649) from the North Fork Sauk River Trailhead (~2,050 ft), reached via Forest Road 49 off the Mountain Loop Highway south of Darrington. The trail climbs gently through old-growth forest along the river valley for about 5.5 miles to Mackinaw Shelter — a possible camp, though tight for a larger party — crossing several tributaries en route, including Red Creek, which parties describe as interesting but not difficult to ford in normal flow (a trekking pole/sturdy stick helps with balance); it can run considerably higher during spring snowmelt or after rain. Past the shelter the trail turns uphill in earnest, climbing roughly 3.2 miles of sustained switchbacks through subalpine forest to a junction with the Pacific Crest Trail in a meadow (~6,000 ft) with the first real views of Glacier Peak and the White Chuck/Kololo massif. Turn right (north) on the PCT and follow it about a quarter mile to White Pass (5,900 ft) — roughly 9 miles and 4,800+ ft of gain from the trailhead, and the last reliable, easy water source before the high traverse. From White Pass the maintained trail ends and the route becomes a boot path: traverse north below the White Mountain ridge into Foam Basin / White River Meadows (~6,300-6,500 ft), the common base camp, either via Red Pass (1.2 miles from the PCT junction) or by crossing snowfields to the notch west of Point 6770 and dropping into the White Chuck River basin (the 'Foam Pass' variant). From camp, climb to Foam Pass and cross the White Chuck Glacier and Glacier Gap onto the White River Glacier — this is glacier travel, and rope/crampons/axe are standard gear here; crevasses are typically open and visible to weave around by late summer but can be harder to read under early-season snow bridges. From the gap, drop a short way onto the White River Glacier and come at the peak from the south, climbing the snow headwall to the summit ridge and an easy talus-and-ledge scramble to the summit (Class 2+). This is a long approach in its own right — the round trip runs roughly 28-30 miles — so almost all parties camp at White River Meadows or Foam Basin rather than attempting the trailhead-to-summit push in a single push. There are two long approaches: this North Fork Sauk line, and the alternate White River Trail approach from the east, which reaches a similar high basin by a comparably long trail-plus-cross-country line.

edits.new: follow it roughly a quarter mile, reaching White Pass (5,900 ft)

text: From the North Fork Sauk Trailhead near 2,050 ft at the end of FR-49, Trail #649 runs about 5.5 miles up the valley on an easy grade through old growth, fording several tributaries. Red Creek is the first crossing that can actually stop you: manageable at normal flow, considerably higher during snowmelt or after rain, and worth a pole. Mackinaw Shelter at 2,950 ft is a possible camp but tight for a big party, and it is where the trail leaves the river — fill water there. Above the shelter the trail climbs about 3.2 miles of sustained switchbacks to a meadow junction with the Pacific Crest Trail near 6,000 ft, then a quarter mile north on the PCT to White Pass at 5,900 ft. That is roughly nine miles and 4,800 ft from the car and the last easy water before the high traverse. Maintained trail ends at the pass. Traverse north below the White Mountain ridge into Foam Basin and White River Meadows around 6,300-6,500 ft — the usual base camp — either by way of Red Pass or by crossing snowfields to the notch west of Point 6770 and dropping into the White Chuck basin. Almost nobody does this from the car in a day, and the round trip is long enough that the two published distances for it disagree.

edits.new: either via Red Pass or by crossing snowfields toward the notch lying west of Point 6770 and descending into the White Chuck basin

text: Kyes Peak (7,280+ ft) is the highest summit of the Monte Cristo group, sharing a remote high basin with Columbia Peak and Monte Cristo Peak that holds the shrinking Columbia Glacier on its north/northeast flank above Blanca Lake. Formerly known as 'Goblin Peak' and 'Mount Michigan,' it was renamed for Rear Admiral James E. Kyes, an Everett native who commanded a destroyer in WWII; two Everett Boy Scouts (Kyes and Reginald Bachelder) made the first recorded ascent on August 15, 1920, with a possible earlier USGS survey ascent by Thomas Gerdine around 1897. The peak sees two common lines to the same summit block: the classic, brushy South Ridge climber's trail above Blanca Lake, and a Columbia Glacier approach that some parties consider the more enjoyable 'real' standard route.

edits.old: is the highest summit of the Monte Cristo group
edits.new: is the Monte Cristo group's highest summit

text: An enjoyable alpine route, and the most direct of the three approaches to Kyes. From the northeast base of the peak (~6,000 ft), Class 3 rock along the climber's-left edge of the Pride Glacier leads to the summit via its southeast corner. Glacier travel (crevasses reported) and route-finding through Quartz Basin's cliff bands on the approach add seriousness beyond the rock grade alone.

text:
The Chockstone Route's start is the anchor point and it is the most unmistakable feature on this side of the mountain: it is obvious, at the base of the massive chasm separating North and South Early Winters Spires. A chasm splitting two spires is not something you can be uncertain about, in any weather where you can see the rock at all.

From there the instruction is two words and a feature: up and left, to a ledge below a clean slab. Clean rock is the marker. This route takes the clean face; the ground either side of it does not read as clean.

So the route is sandwiched, and you can bound it both ways: the Chockstone Route is to its right, in the chasm. The west face is to its left. If you are in the chasm you have not left the shared start; if you have traversed all the way left to the shared start with the Northwest Corner, you have gone past.

Confirm by what you are standing on: a ledge, below a slab. Not a chimney, not a corner.

Descent, and it is not a reversal: rappel down the Chockstone Route line, using the same bolted stations that route uses, rather than reversing the Labor Pains pitches. That means you finish where you started, back at the chasm.

edits.new: you can't miss it, at the foot of the huge chasm dividing the North and South Early Winters Spires

text: Walk Stevens Canyon Road west about half a mile to its 90-degree bend, then drop south through open forest to Tatoosh Creek at about 4,500 ft. Stay low into the basin under Lane Peak's north face rather than climbing right toward the south-face saddle, cross the debris apron, and from its top angle left into the Zipper, the middle of three couloirs: about 1,000 ft of 40 to 45 degree snow with short steps to a dead tree at a notch in the east ridge.

text: Same trailhead as the Classic Route: park at the Reflection Lake pullout on Stevens Canyon Road when it's open, or at the Narada Falls pullout in winter/spring when the road is snow-gated (a short, steep ~200 ft climb from Narada Falls regains the road). Walk the road about half a mile to the 90-degree bend, then drop south through open forest toward Tatoosh Creek (~4,500 ft), as with the Classic Route. Rather than climbing right toward the south-face saddle, stay low and work into the basin directly below Lane Peak's north face — the Zipper is the obvious left-leaning couloir splitting the center of the face, visible from the road. From the basin, hike up and across a large triangular apron of avalanche/rockfall debris fanning down from the base of the couloir. From the top of this debris cone, angle climber's left and climb roughly 1,000 ft up the couloir itself to a dead tree at a notch in the peak's east ridge, which marks the top of the technical climbing and the rappel/tie-in point. Snow conditions range from styrofoam neve to alpine ice depending on season and aspect; the basin and lower couloir cross avalanche-prone terrain, so this is a start-early, check-the-forecast approach, especially in winter/spring when most ascents happen. Total approach is roughly 2-2.5 miles one-way from the road to the notch; no water past Tatoosh Creek. In the couloir itself, expect the angle to build from about 40° to 45° near the top, the walls narrowing from roughly 40 ft to 20 ft wide, and up to three short ice/mixed steps (about 15 ft, 8 ft, and a 25 ft crux) depending on fill.

Walk the road about half a mile to the 90-degree bend, then drop south through open forest toward Tatoosh Creek at about 4,500 ft. Rather than climbing right toward the south-face saddle, stay low and work into the basin directly below Lane Peak's north face.

From the basin, hike up and across a large triangular apron of avalanche and rockfall debris fanning down from the base of the couloirs. From the top of that debris cone, angle climber's left and climb roughly 1,000 ft of couloir to a dead tree at a notch in the peak's east ridge, which marks the top of the technical climbing and the rappel point.

Roughly 2 to 2.5 miles one-way with about 2,000 ft of gain to the notch, and no water past Tatoosh Creek. The basin and lower couloir cross avalanche terrain, so this is a start-early, read-the-forecast approach.

text:
Left to right on this face the three couloirs are: Lover's Lane, the Zipper, the Fly. Learn that order before you leave the car. All three drop onto the same debris apron and on a busy weekend all three have parties on them at once, which means overhead hazard from other people as well as from the mountain.

The Zipper is the middle one, and it is the one that leans left and splits the centre of the face. From the top of the debris cone, angle climber's left. If you are working right, you are heading for the Fly.

The strongest test is width, and it is a thing you feel rather than see: the Zipper narrows. About 40 ft wide at the base, closing to about 20 ft near the top. The Fly is broad — 40 to 50 ft — and it stays broad. If the walls are not closing in on you as you gain height, you are in the Fly, one couloir to your right, on easier ground than you came for.

The second test is countable and it is the one that settles it: the Zipper has up to three short steps — about 15 ft, then about 8 ft, then a 25 ft crux near the top. The Fly has none worth the name. If you have climbed a thousand feet of continuous 45-degree snow and met no step at all, you are not in the Zipper.

The top-out is an object, which is the best kind of confirmation: a dead tree at a notch in the east ridge. That tree carries the fixed rappel slings. If you have topped out onto open ridge with no tree, you are on something else — Lover's Lane finishes on the ridge above this notch, and the Fly finishes at the west-ridge notch.

What the angle should do: build from about 40 degrees to about 45 near the top. It does not exceed that. Ground steeper than 45 sustained means Lover's Lane, which reaches about 60.

text: From a base camp between the two Yang Yang Lakes, the route heads south around a forested ridge and ascends talus to a distinctive 'secret stair' — a precipitous path up compacted dirt and rock through a small gully to a grassy ledge. From there it follows the ridgeline to a rock outcropping beneath Le Conte's North Face, then works around (avoiding) Peak 7004 via east-slope talus and snow before an exposed traverse of narrow, loose ledges gains the summit. Rated class 4 scrambling; a rope, ice axe, and crampons are standard given the glacier travel required just to reach the peak.

text: The stair starts where the ridge rises sharply and falls away on its north side. Climb the trail and talus up the forested ridge and watch the crest: at the point where it rears up and drops off on the right, or north, side, a precipitous path of compacted dirt and rock leads up through a small gully to a grassy ledge fifteen to twenty feet wide. Walk west along that ledge and make a full 180-degree turn at its far end to pick up the path to the top of the ridge — that reversal is what earns it the name, and if the ledge you are on runs out with no way to double back, it is not the stair. Follow the ridge to a rock outcropping immediately beneath Le Conte's north face; this is where parties drop their packs and it is the base of the climb proper. Peak 7004 is a hump on the ridge that is very hard to get around directly: bypass it on its east slope. Above, a loose rock gully gains a ridge on the north side and short steep snow near 7,200 ft leads to the east notch, then a quick, exposed traverse of a narrow ledge to the top.

text:
The arrival is a rock step, called a chute in published descriptions, and it sits below the main summit after you have crossed the glacier basin and traversed north under Lemah Two.

The touchable sequence at the step, from a party who did it: pass a small waterfall, climb a wet gully for about ten feet, then work right onto dry rock. Those ten feet are the fourth-class move and the landing beneath them is relatively safe. That waterfall-then-wet-gully-then-step-right is the thing to look for; it is the crux of the whole climb and it is where the approach ends.

There is a tempting alternative that does not work: a ramp far to the left looks as though it would let you bypass the rock step entirely, but reaching it means an unpleasant moat crossing, and the party that looked at it came back down and took the step.

Above the step, the recorded mistake is worth more than the recorded route. Between Lemah Two and Lemah Three there is a small snowfield. A published sketch puts the line just left of the summit rocks, and following that into a mostly snow-filled gully leads to a difficult top, a snow bridge onto loose rock, and about a hundred feet of loose third and fourth class. The party who did that found on the way down that the honest instruction is simply: gain the ridge where it looks easiest. It is.

One route people have taken and should not repeat: descending a gully from Lemah One to reach the glacier. It melts out into very unstable talus blocks.

The Spectacle Lake approach is documented but has been explicitly superseded — the slide area between the lake outlet and the shoulder has grown into ten- to twelve-foot slide alder on a thirty-degree slope, dense enough that you cannot see over it to aim at anything.

edits.old: gain the ridge where it looks easiest. It is.
edits.new: gain the ridge wherever it appears easiest. And it is.

text: The workhorse camp of the entire western half of this zone. From the trailhead at the north end of Cooper Lake the trail runs about four gentle miles along the Cooper River to Pete Lake, and roughly two and a half more to the Lemah Meadows area and the Pacific Crest Trail junction. Parties bound for Lemah Mountain and Lemah Two leave the trail here and follow a climbers' path up the north side of Lemah Creek past waterfalls to the meadow at about 3,600 ft, where the creek spreads into shallow ponds; camp at the far end, and expect a thicket of slide alder that is best turned in the timber to the north rather than fought through. Parties bound for Chimney Rock also pass through, but leave the PCT further north — see the Chimney Glacier basin entry. Pete Lake itself is low, forested and mosquito-ridden in early summer, and it is a long way from any summit, so it works as a first-night camp or a bail-out rather than a climbing base. Season is roughly July into October; the valley clears early but the basins above hold snow well into July. The Cooper River road is paved then gravel and passenger-car friendly. Honest caveat for 2026: the Pete Lake trail was inside a large wildfire closure on the Cle Elum Ranger District through late summer, with the closure scheduled to run to the end of October and subject to change — confirm the trail is open before driving out.

text: Day 1 follows the well-graded Lena Lake Trail 3 miles to Lena Lake, then a steep, primitive trail up West Fork Lena Creek to Upper Lena Lake (6.5 mi, 4,000 ft gain from the trailhead). Day 2 leaves the trail entirely: climb southwest across meadows/heather toward the ridge south of Mt Lena, follow intermittent way trails west past Scout Lake, over Scout Pass (5,200 ft) and Upper Scout Lake/Scout Basin, over Ullin's Pass (5,000 ft, with views of the 'Ullin's Bathtubs' tarns), then up the steep snow/dirt 'St. Peter's Ramp' to St. Peter's Gate (5,950 ft) — the high point of the traverse and an obvious notch in Mt Stone's SE ridge. Lake of the Angels lies half a mile southwest of the gate in a grassy bowl. The optional Mt Stone summit side-trip climbs a class 3-4 gully on the mountain's south face to a rock bowl, joins the standard west-ridge route, and finishes with a class 2-3 scramble on solid pillow basalt to the summit (about 1,100 ft gain round trip, ~3 hrs). Day 3 descends the Putvin Trail — historic and primitive, with cliff sections (one with a fixed handline, one requiring tree roots) past Whitehorse Basin and the Pond of the False Prophet — to the Putvin Trailhead, about 4 miles by road from the Lena Lake Trailhead where the trip began.

text: From the Blue Lake Trailhead (FS Trail #314, ~5,400 ft, on SR-20 about 1 mile west of Washington Pass), follow the maintained, well-graded Blue Lake Trail through forest and open meadow for about 1.7 miles to a small meadow just past a small stream crossing (the last reliable water). Leave the maintained trail here on a climbers' boot path heading left (east), ascending through granite slabs, talus, and heather meadow toward the gully that drops from the notch between Liberty Bell and Concord Tower. The path is steep in places with short sections of 3rd-class scrambling. At a fork roughly 200 ft below the notch, stay left to reach the Liberty Bell-Concord Tower notch (~7,300 ft) — about 2 miles and ~2,100 ft of gain total from the car, 1.5-2.5 hours. The approach gully commonly holds snow into late June, so carry an ice axe (and possibly crampons) for an early-season ascent.

text: This is the standard descent line for most Liberty Bell summit routes, not just the Beckey Route itself. From the summit, downclimb the upper (4th) pitch about 20 ft to the first ledge, then go left (east) to a tree hung with rappel slings. One single-rope rappel with a 60m rope reaches a flatter area; from the bolted anchor there, one double-rope rappel (or two single-rope rappels if only carrying one rope) reaches the Liberty Bell-Concord notch. From the notch, downclimb the loose approach gully back to the climbers' path and the Blue Lake Trail. All anchors are bolted or fixed tree slings — no natural gear or v-thread anchors are needed.

text:
Standard East Face approach: park at the pond pullout near the hairpin turn east of Washington Pass, and follow the cairned climbers' path from the pond's east end about a mile to the East Face talus.

Fourteen pitches. Although it is technically the easiest all-free route up the East Face, the route takes about one and a half times as much effort as Liberty Crack, on often poor rock and gear, and apart from where it intersects Liberty Crack there are no bolted belay stances.

text:
This is the only route on the east face that starts to the left of Liberty Crack, and that makes it the easiest start on the wall to confirm by elimination. It begins at a loose corner system about 100 ft left of Liberty Crack.

So the test is directional and countable: from Liberty Crack, walk left roughly 100 ft to a corner system. Every other line here is to the right of Liberty Crack. If you are walking right along the base, you are walking away from this route, and everything you meet in that direction belongs to something else: Freedom or Death, Thin Red Line, Liberty and Injustice for All, Live Free or Die and the Independence Route in that order.

And Liberty Crack itself is found by traversing 40 ft left on third and fourth class ledges from the base of the talus, so this route is roughly 140 ft of leftward travel from where the path meets the rock.

A hardware test that cuts the other way from the rest of this face: there are no bolted belay stances on this route except where it crosses Liberty Crack. Several of its neighbours are fully bolted. If you reach a bolted anchor early, you are probably not on Freedom Rider.

What to expect so you do not second-guess the find: the corner system is described as loose, and the rock and gear on the route generally as often poor. Poor rock at the start is consistent with this line, not evidence you are off it.

Descent: the shared East Face rappel line into Beckey Gully, or downclimbing the sheltered Beckey Route slab in good conditions. Both put you on the west side of the mountain, away from the East Face pullout.

edits.new: Its start is a loose corner system roughly 100 ft to the left of Liberty Crack.

text:
Stop short of the notch. A couple of hundred vertical feet below the top of the Liberty-Concord notch, locate a side gully on climber's left with a large cave in it. Walk partway up that side gully, then move right onto a treed ledge to start.

So there are three things to find and all three are tactile rather than visual: a side gully on the left, a large cave inside it, and a ledge with trees on its right-hand side. Trees on a ledge are unmistakable underfoot.

The negative test is the most useful line here, because the error is always the same one: if you have reached the notch, you have gone roughly two hundred feet too far. This route leaves the main gully below its top. Everything at the notch itself belongs to the Beckey Route, Overexposure and the standard descent.

A second route shares the cave, so the ledge is what separates them: Sidewinder also scrambles to a major shelf or ramp below the cave feature. This route goes partway up the side gully and then steps right onto the treed ledge. Below the cave is Sidewinder's ground; up and right of it is this one.

Where it goes: three pitches rejoining the Beckey Route near its top, then the standard two single-rope rappels off chains to the notch and the gully back to the trail.

text:
The route starts right at the top of the notch between Liberty Bell and Concord Tower, and specifically it begins above the notch rather than at it. That distinction is the whole find: Beckey Route parties stop at the notch and start climbing from it. This route asks for a little extra scrambling up from the notch into the initial belay.

Which notch, because there are two on this ridge and they are only a few hundred feet apart: the Liberty Bell-Concord notch, at about 7,300 ft, is the one this route uses. The Concord-Lexington notch is further along and serves Concord's south face and Lexington's north face. The discriminating test at the top of the gully is what the wall in front of you offers: the Liberty Bell-Concord notch faces a crack system. The Concord-Lexington notch gives onto low-angle, gravelly ledges.

So: crack system in front of you at the top of the gully means you are at the right notch for this route.

Confirm by the length of the climb, which is short and countable: four pitches at Grade II 5.8, and the second pitch tops out at the same bolted anchor system that starts the standard Liberty Bell descent. Most parties either stop there or continue a few hundred feet of fourth and low-fifth scrambling to the true summit. If you have climbed four pitches and are nowhere near a bolted descent anchor, you are not on this route.

Budget extra time and care for the scramble into the first belay compared with Beckey Route parties, because it is exposed and it is where this route differs.

text:
The route is climber's right of Liberty Crack, and the published method for finding it is to work downward from the features above rather than along the base. Look climber's right of Liberty Crack and connect the line down from the features higher on the wall. Some mellow snow travel is usually necessary to reach the base.

So this is the one east face route whose start is honestly described as a sighting problem, and that is worth knowing before the cloud comes down. Fix the line from the talus while you can see the wall. If you cannot see the wall, you cannot locate this start by walking the base, and no description will change that.

What you can do without a view is bound it, because the order along the base is known. Left to right: Freedom Rider about 100 ft left of Liberty Crack, Liberty Crack, Freedom or Death just right of it on a leftward-trending ramp with bolts above, Thin Red Line, Liberty and Injustice for All about 10 m right of Thin Red Line, Live Free or Die, and the Independence Route at the far right or north edge of the face beneath a red roof and alcove called the Baer Ceiling about 85 m up.

So: if you are standing at a leftward-trending ramp with bolts above it, you are one route left, on Freedom or Death. If you can see a red roof about 85 M above you, you have walked all the way right to the Independence Route.

The descent decides which car you end at, and this route has both options: from the top of the route near M&M Ledge, work climber's left to good bolts and make four double-rope rappels essentially to the ground at the base of the East Face, returning to your pack and the East Face approach. If you instead continue to the true summit and take the standard Liberty Bell notch descent, you finish on the west side of the mountain and need a shuttle or a road walk back.

edits.new: Reaching the base usually takes some mellow snow travel.

text: Liberty Ridge splits the North Face of Mount Rainier between Willis Wall and Liberty Wall, two of the most dangerous alpine walls in the lower 48 states. The route is considered the premier unguided climb on Mount Rainier and is included in Roper and Steck's Fifty Classic Climbs in North America. Approximately 100 climbers attempt Liberty Ridge annually; however, the route accounts for roughly 25% of Mount Rainier climbing fatalities due to persistent objective hazards and the committing nature of the climb. Fast, experienced parties can complete the climb in two days, while average parties typically require three to four days. Early-season timing (May to mid-June) is critical to minimize rockfall and avalanche hazard as temperatures warm and snow/ice conditions deteriorate.

edits.new: Liberty Ridge divides the North Face of Mount Rainier between Willis Wall and Liberty Wall, and those two walls are among the deadliest alpine faces in the lower 48 states.

text: Move out onto the east face of the ridge to get past the Black Pyramid, on exposed snow and ice up to about 60 degrees, with the angle easing back to 30 to 40 once you are around it. Several pitches of 40 to 60 degree ice and steep glacier ground then gain the Liberty Cap Glacier at around 13,500 ft. The bergschrund below the cap is usually the crux and varies year to year from a walk up a ramp to a short vertical ice step; the bridges and icy ledges across it are seasonal, so plan to climb it rather than count on finding a way over. Easier snow leads to the top.

text: From Thumb Rock, ascend either a short vertical ice pitch (70-80 degrees) in the center of the rock band, or traverse left around the cliff. It is one of the steepest steps on the route and is where parties often spend significant time; the summit bergschrund higher up is usually the technical crux.
